task.title: Does Comet Browser Run on Raspberry Pi

user_message.content: does comet browser run on raspberry pie

status_update.description: Manus is working on your request

assistant_message.content: Let me research whether Comet Browser can run on Raspberry Pi for you.

**No, Comet Browser does not run on Raspberry Pi.**

Comet Browser (by Perplexity AI) is a Chromium-based, AI-powered web browser that is currently only officially supported on:

- **Windows 10 and 11** (64-bit x64 and ARM64)
- **macOS 13 (Ventura) or later** (Intel and Apple Silicon)

According to Perplexity's official help center, Comet Browser is **not officially supported** on:

- Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian, Mint, Red Hat, etc.)
- ChromeOS (Chromebooks)
- iOS and Android devices (though mobile apps exist separately)
- Other systems such as BSD, Solaris, HarmonyOS, KaiOS, etc.

Since Raspberry Pi runs a Linux-based operating system (typically Raspberry Pi OS, which is Debian-based) on ARM processors, it falls squarely into the unsupported category. Additionally, the minimum system requirements call for an Intel or AMD 64-bit processor (or Apple Silicon), 4 GB of RAM, and a 1280x800 display — specs that many Raspberry Pi models would struggle to meet.

**In short:** There is no version of Comet Browser available for Raspberry Pi, and it is unlikely to work even through unofficial means given the OS and architecture constraints.

Source: [Comet Browser OS Requirements (Perplexity Help Center)](https://comet-help.perplexity.ai/en/articles/11734730-operating-system-requirements)

assistant_message.content: Great question! Let me research which web browsers are available and work well on Raspberry Pi.

Here are the web browsers that **do** run on Raspberry Pi:

---

### Full-Featured GUI Browsers

| Browser | Engine | Best For | Pi Model | Install |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Chromium** | Chromium | General browsing, kiosk setups | Pi 4, Pi 5 (usable on Pi 3) | `sudo apt install chromium-browser` (pre-installed on Pi OS) |
| **Firefox** | Gecko | Syncing, privacy, extensions | Pi 4, Pi 5 | `sudo apt install firefox` (now pre-installed on Pi OS) |
| **Brave** | Chromium | Privacy, ad/tracker blocking | Pi 4, Pi 5 | `curl -fsS https://dl.brave.com/install.sh \| sh` |
| **Vivaldi** | Chromium | Power users, deep customization | Pi 4, Pi 5 | Via Pi-Apps or Ubuntu repo |

**Chromium** is the default and generally fastest browser on Raspberry Pi — it has been specifically optimized by the Raspberry Pi Foundation with hardware acceleration on Pi 4/5. **Firefox** is the only major non-Chromium option and is great if you want to sync bookmarks/passwords with your PC, though it's heavier. **Brave** is excellent for privacy with built-in ad blocking. **Vivaldi** is for power users who love customization.

---

### Lightweight / Niche GUI Browsers

| Browser | Engine | Best For | Pi Model |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Epiphany (GNOME Web)** | WebKit | Simple browsing, low overhead | Pi 3, Pi Zero |
| **Midori** | WebKit | Minimalist browsing | Pi 3, Pi Zero |
| **Dillo** | Custom | Ultra-lightweight, basic HTML | Pi Zero, Pi 1 |
| **Surf** | WebKit | Minimalist, suckless philosophy | Pi Zero, Pi 3 |
| **LuaKit** | WebKit | Scriptable, ultra-lightweight | Pi Zero, Pi 3 |
| **Kweb** | WebKit | Kiosk mode specifically | Any Pi |

These are ideal for older or lower-spec Pi models (Pi Zero, Pi 3, or earlier). They won't handle modern JavaScript-heavy websites well, but they're great for static pages, dashboards, local network tools, and kiosk displays.

---

### Privacy Browser

| Browser | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Tor Browser** | Can be installed on 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS. Heavy on resources but provides anonymity. |

---

### Terminal / Text-Based Browsers

| Browser | Install | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Lynx** | `sudo apt install lynx` | Classic text-only browser, extremely fast |
| **w3m** | `sudo apt install w3m` | Text browser with inline image support |
| **Links / ELinks** | `sudo apt install links` | Text browser with optional graphics mode |

These run entirely in the terminal with virtually zero overhead — perfect for headless Pi setups, SSH sessions, or when you just need to quickly look something up.

---

### Quick Recommendation

- **Pi 5 or Pi 4 (4+ GB RAM):** Chromium, Firefox, Brave, or Vivaldi — all work well
- **Pi 3 or Pi 4 (2 GB RAM):** Chromium is your best bet; Firefox is usable but slower
- **Pi Zero or Pi 1/2:** Stick with lightweight options like Epiphany, Dillo, or terminal browsers (Lynx, w3m)

user_message.content: List the best browsers for a Raspberry Pi Zero.

status_update.description: Manus is working on your request

assistant_message.content: Good question! The Pi Zero is very resource-constrained, so the browser options are quite different. Let me research this specifically.

The Raspberry Pi Zero is very resource-constrained (only 512 MB RAM), so browser choice matters a lot. Here are the best options, ranked from most to least recommended:

---

### Important: Which Pi Zero Do You Have?

| Model | CPU | RAM | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pi Zero / Zero W** | Single-core ARM11 @ 1 GHz (32-bit) | 512 MB | Very limited; only lightweight browsers are practical |
| **Pi Zero 2 W** | Quad-core Cortex-A53 @ 1 GHz (64-bit) | 512 MB | Much better CPU, but still only 512 MB RAM |

---

### Best GUI Browsers for Pi Zero

**1. Epiphany (GNOME Web)** — Best overall pick for Pi Zero

Epiphany uses roughly 40-65% less RAM than Chromium (~214 MB idle vs. ~627 MB for Chromium). It was actually the official Raspberry Pi browser before Chromium took over. It supports modern web standards via WebKit and writes almost nothing to the SD card, extending its lifespan.

Install: `sudo apt install epiphany-browser`

**2. NetSurf** — Best for ultra-low resource usage

NetSurf uses its own custom rendering engine and is extremely lightweight. The trade-off is no JavaScript support, so many modern sites won't work fully. But for Wikipedia, forums, documentation, and basic HTML pages, it's excellent on the Pi Zero.

Install: May need to compile from source or grab packages from [NetSurf CI builds](https://ci.netsurf-browser.org/)

**3. Dillo** — Fastest raw browsing, minimal features

Dillo is an ultra-lightweight browser (only ~1.6 MB binary) that is blazing fast on even the original Pi Zero. No JavaScript and limited CSS support, but if you just need to read text-based web pages, nothing is faster.

Install: `sudo apt install dillo`

**4. Links2 (graphical mode)** — Graphical browsing with ~5 MB RAM

Links2 can run in a graphical mode that displays images while using only about 5 MB of memory. It's an incredible option for the Pi Zero when you want to see images but can't afford a full browser's overhead.

Install: `sudo apt install links2`
Run in graphical mode: `links2 -g`

**5. Kweb** — Best for kiosk / dedicated display setups

Kweb was built specifically for Raspberry Pi kiosk mode. It's WebKit-based and supports audio, video, playlists, and even YouTube. If you're using your Pi Zero to display a dashboard or a single webpage, this is purpose-built for that.

**6. Midori** — Lightweight but aging

Midori is a minimalist WebKit browser that can run on the Pi Zero, but its performance and feature set have fallen behind. Extensions don't work well, and speed test results are disappointing even compared to other lightweight options.

---

### Best Terminal / Text-Based Browsers for Pi Zero

These run entirely in the terminal and use almost no resources — ideal for SSH sessions or headless setups:

| Browser | RAM Usage | Features | Install |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lynx** | ~2-3 MB | Text-only, keyboard navigation, extremely fast | `sudo apt install lynx` |
| **w3m** | ~3-5 MB | Text with inline image support, tables render well | `sudo apt install w3m` |
| **Links / ELinks** | ~3-5 MB | Text mode with optional graphics, good table support | `sudo apt install links` |

---

### Browsers to Avoid on Pi Zero

| Browser | Why |
|---|---|
| **Firefox** | Uses ~600 MB RAM at idle — that alone exceeds the Pi Zero's total RAM |
| **Chromium** | Uses ~627 MB+ at idle; CPU pegged at 100% on Pi Zero; barely usable even on Pi Zero 2 W |
| **Brave** | High memory footprint, too heavy |
| **Vivaldi** | Even heavier than Chromium due to extra features |

---

### Quick Recommendation

- **For general web browsing on Pi Zero 2 W:** Start with **Epiphany** — it's the best balance of modern web support and low resource usage.
- **For basic/static pages on any Pi Zero:** **Dillo** or **NetSurf** — lightning fast, but limited modern web support.
- **For a kiosk or dashboard display:** **Kweb** — purpose-built for this.
- **For terminal/SSH use:** **Lynx** or **w3m** — virtually zero overhead.

user_message.content: List the installation steps for compiling NetSurf from source on a Raspberry Pi Zero.

status_update.description: Manus is working on your request

assistant_message.content: Let me research the exact steps for compiling NetSurf from source on a Raspberry Pi Zero.

Here is the complete step-by-step guide for compiling NetSurf from source on a Raspberry Pi Zero. I've attached it as a document for easy reference, but here's a summary of the 8 steps:

1. **Increase the swap file** from 100 MB to at least 1024 MB (edit `/etc/dphys-swapfile`) — this is critical or the Pi Zero will freeze during compilation.
2. **Download the build environment script** (`env.sh`) from the official NetSurf repository.
3. **Install all build dependencies** using the `ns-package-install` command provided by the script.
4. **Clone the source code** for the browser and all its libraries using `ns-clone`.
5. **Build and install the project libraries** (HTML parser, CSS engine, etc.) using `ns-pull-install`.
6. **Switch to the new workspace** and source the updated environment script.
7. **Compile the browser** — either `make` for the GTK desktop version, or `make TARGET=framebuffer` if you're running without a desktop environment.
8. **Run NetSurf** with `./nsgtk3` (GTK) or `./nsfb` (framebuffer).

**Important warnings:** The entire process will take several hours on a Pi Zero due to its single-core CPU. On a Pi Zero 2 W (quad-core), it will be faster but still slow. If compiling proves too difficult, pre-built packages are available from the [NetSurf CI server](https://ci.netsurf-browser.org/debian/buster/armhf/).

The attached guide includes full commands, troubleshooting tips, and references to the official documentation.

user_message.content: if raspberry pi is already running on our server - how do i locate it and make edits

status_update.description: Manus is working on your request

assistant_message.content: Great question! Let me research the best methods for locating a Raspberry Pi on your network and connecting to it for remote management.

Here's a complete guide (also attached as a document). There are two parts: **finding the Pi** and **connecting to edit it**.

---

### Part 1: Locating the Pi on Your Network

| Method | Command / Action | When to Use |
|---|---|---|
| **mDNS Ping** | `ping raspberrypi.local` | Easiest — works if mDNS is enabled (default on Pi OS) |
| **Router Admin Page** | Visit `192.168.1.1` in a browser, check "Connected Devices" | When you have router access |
| **Nmap Network Scan** | `sudo nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24` | When you can't access the router; look for MAC addresses starting with `B8:27:EB`, `D0:3B:FF`, or `DC:A6:32` |

---

### Part 2: Connecting and Making Edits

| Method | Best For | How |
|---|---|---|
| **SSH** | Quick command-line edits | `ssh username@192.168.1.42`, then use `nano` or `vim` to edit files |
| **VNC** | Full graphical desktop access | Enable VNC on the Pi, then connect with RealVNC Viewer |
| **SFTP / SCP** | Transferring files back and forth | Use FileZilla, WinSCP, or `scp` on the command line |
| **VS Code Remote SSH** | Developer-friendly editing with a full IDE | Install the "Remote - SSH" extension in VS Code, connect to the Pi |

---

### Quick Start (Most Common Path)

If SSH is already enabled on the Pi, you can likely connect right now:

```bash
ssh username@raspberrypi.local
```

Once connected, navigate to the file you want to edit and open it:

```bash
nano /path/to/your/file.txt
```

If you're unsure whether SSH is enabled, or if you need the full graphical desktop, the attached guide covers all the options in detail.

user_message.content: can you set up raspberry pi to take voice commands? for example, if I have a browser that I have named "Vacancy Report" could I set up Alexa to switch to a different page in the browser named "Manager KPI Performance"?

status_update.description: Manus is working on your request

assistant_message.content: Great question! Let me research how to set up voice commands on a Raspberry Pi — specifically using Alexa to control browser navigation between different pages. This is a really interesting use case.

**Yes, you can absolutely do this!** The attached guide covers three approaches in detail, but here's the summary:

---

### Three Ways to Voice-Control Your Pi's Browser

| Approach | Difficulty | Requires | Voice Command Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Node-RED + Alexa** (Recommended) | Easy-Medium | Amazon Echo, Node-RED on Pi | *"Alexa, turn on Manager KPI Performance"* |
| **Flask API + Alexa Skill** | Medium | Amazon Echo, Python on Pi, network access | *"Alexa, show Manager KPI"* (via custom routine) |
| **Vosk Offline Voice** | Medium-Hard | USB microphone on Pi, no Echo needed | *"Show Manager KPI"* (spoken directly to the Pi) |

---

### How It Works (Big Picture)

The flow is the same regardless of approach:

> **Your voice** → **Voice service recognizes the command** → **Signal sent to the Pi** → **Script changes the browser URL**

The key trick for that last step is launching Chromium with **remote debugging** enabled:

```bash
chromium-browser --kiosk --remote-debugging-port=9222 http://your-server/vacancy-report
```

This lets any script instantly change the displayed page without touching the keyboard.

---

### My Recommendation for Your Use Case

Since you're running dashboards like "Vacancy Report" and "Manager KPI Performance," the **Node-RED + Alexa** approach is the best fit. You would:

1. Install Node-RED on the Pi
2. Install the `node-red-contrib-alexa-home` plugin (emulates smart home devices locally)
3. Create virtual devices named after your dashboards
4. Say *"Alexa, discover devices"*
5. Then simply say *"Alexa, turn on Manager KPI Performance"* to switch pages

No Amazon developer account, no AWS Lambda, no cloud setup required — it all runs locally on your network.

The full guide with code examples and step-by-step instructions is attached.
